slots.title: US–Venezuela oil pact framed as 25 years
slots.body:
Reuters quotes interim President Delcy Rodriguez: the U.S. energy deal would stay in force for 25 years and aim for 1.5 million barrels per day of output while keeping sovereignty over natural resources.

The Wall Street Journal, citing people involved in talks, reported the U.S. government plans a 35% passive stake in Alejandro Betancourt’s North American Blue Energy Partners.

Brent crude settled at $88.10 on the prior session, down 0.5%.

What part of the supply story are you tracking first — the 25-year framework or the reported stake structure?

slots.title: Bessent warns on disorderly yen moves
slots.body:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said disorderly yen moves can trigger forced unwinds that risk destabilizing global markets.

He tied that to higher borrowing costs for U.S. households and businesses.

The Nikkei 225 finished the prior overseas session up 0.4%, at 66,405.56.

The dollar proxy in the data (UUP) closed up 0.6%, at $28.18.

How do you usually connect currency volatility headlines to rates and credit?

slots.title: US cash session recap — Aug. 29, 2026
slots.body:
The S&P 500 finished at 7,711.76, down 0.2% (-19.23 points), after trading between 7,700.91 and 7,771.48.
The benchmark still sits below its 52-week high of 7,816.70 in the injected data.

The Nasdaq Composite lost 0.5%, closing at 26,402.42 (-138.93 points), with a session range of 26,359.27 to 26,700.68.
Tech-heavy exposure showed more drag than the broad large-cap index.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average was nearly flat at 53,559.99 (-9.45 points, 0.0%).
Large industrials did not mirror the Nasdaq’s decline to the same degree.

The Russell 2000 fell 1.4% to 2,972.37 (-41.97 points), hitting the session low at 2,972.37.
Small-cap weakness was the clearest index story in the injected set.

The calendar flagged the Jackson Hole Symposium (US, high impact) on Aug. 29.
Coverage in the injected feed centered on Fed Chair Kevin Warsh’s Jackson Hole remarks and what they imply for rate guidance and market volatility.

NVIDIA closed at 217.55, down 4.6%, with a day low of 216.82 and very high share volume in the mega-cap block.
Advanced Micro Devices fell 2.3% to 465.58; Taiwan Semiconductor fell 2.3% to 417.52; ASML fell 2.2% to 1,696.16 — a coordinated chip-complex pullback alongside Nvidia.

Amazon rose 4.0% to 266.43 (high 267.56).
Microsoft rose 1.7% to 513.53.
Alphabet Class A rose 1.7% to 346.59; Class C Google rose 1.5% to 342.88.
Apple rose 1.6% to 319.70.
Those gains partially offset chip pressure in the megacap basket.

Tesla closed at 348.75, down 1.7%.
Broadcom slipped 0.7% to 368.79.
Bank of America rose 1.9% to 62.32.
Elastic (ESTC) was up 19.3% to 99.91 among liquid gainers in the injected screen.

Gold futures (GCUSD) settled at 4,529.90, down 2.9% (-134.10), with a session low of 4,495.00.
Brent crude (BZUSD) was 88.10, down 0.5%; the USO ETF proxy for oil was 129.70, down 0.2%.

The UUP dollar-bullish ETF proxy rose 0.6% to 28.18; EUR/USD was 1.16, down 0.6%.
Bitcoin (BTCUSD) was 78,177.68, down 0.1%.

The VIX closed at 14.43, down 0.6% (range 14.13–14.84).
Injected Treasury snapshot (dated 2026-08-27): 10-year yield 4.7%, 2s10s spread 0.47.

Overseas references in the bundle: Nikkei 225 +0.4% to 66,405.56; FTSE 100 +0.3% to 10,824.26; Hang Seng -0.3% to 25,584.80.
The earnings calendar in the injection was empty for this run — no fresh reported actuals to tie to single-stock moves.

slots.title: August jobs print lands Friday at 12:30 p.m.
slots.body:
August U.S. employment data is scheduled for Friday, Sept. 4, at 12:30 p.m.
ET.

Nonfarm payrolls carry a consensus estimate of 45K jobs added; July printed at -23K.

The unemployment rate is expected at 4.2%, up from 4.1% in July.

Private payrolls are estimated at 50K versus 30K prior.

Average hourly earnings are estimated +0.2% month over month and +3.3% year over year.

The release counts hiring across the economy and is often read alongside wage figures as a read on labor demand.

Which line in the report do you watch first — headline jobs, unemployment, or wages?
